subsection.title: Derivative table
subsection.p: The main elementary derivative formulas from this chapter are collected below. Each formula is valid on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable.

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

exercise.title: Why do implicit and inverse derivatives reverse two different things?

statement.p: Implicit differentiation treats y as changing because x changes, even with no formula y=f(x). The inverse rule reverses a graph and therefore reverses slope. In your own words, why are those two ideas related to the chain rule, yet not the same task?

hint.p: One starts from a relation and solves for dy/dx. The other starts from a reversible function and takes the reciprocal slope at the matching point.

subsection.p: At
the derivative is 0. The graph has horizontal tangents there. One is a high point nearby; the other is a low point nearby.
That observation opens the next part of the book.

Derivatives compute slopes. But slopes tell us when a function rises, when it falls, where it turns, and where it bends. The next chapter asks how much of a graph we can understand from its derivative.

exercise.title: Why is a computed derivative already information about shape?

statement.p: The sign of f' tells where a graph rises or falls, and a zero of f' marks a horizontal tangent. In your own words, why was this chapter’s working language built not only to compute more derivatives, but to prepare for reading a graph from its slopes?

hint.p: A derivative is local slope information. Collected point by point, those slopes begin to describe the whole curve.
